title: Safe Clinical AI
summary: Building AI systems that are reliable enough for medical practice — not just impressive on benchmarks.
argument: A mistake in a language model demo is annoying. A mistake in clinical decision support can cause direct harm. This asymmetry demands a different standard — one that the AI field has not yet settled on how to meet.

Neryva's clinical AI program starts from a simple premise: reliability in clinical settings is not just a matter of accuracy on held-out datasets. It requires systems that fail predictably, communicate their uncertainty honestly, and remain consistent across the full distribution of patients and conditions that appear in real medical practice — including the edge cases that benchmarks rarely capture. We study what building such systems actually requires, and where current methods fall short.

threads.title: Reliability Under Distribution Shift
threads.question: How do we build clinical AI systems that degrade gracefully — and audibly — when inputs fall outside the training distribution rather than failing silently?

threads.title: Human-AI Collaboration
threads.question: How should clinical AI systems communicate uncertainty to practitioners in a way that improves, rather than undermines, clinical judgment at the point of decision?

threads.title: Validation in Edge Cases
threads.question: What evaluation protocols are necessary to adequately cover the long tail of clinical scenarios that determine real-world reliability but are underrepresented in standard benchmarks?

currentWork: Reviewing validation methodologies across existing clinical AI deployments and identifying the most common failure modes in evaluation design. Building a taxonomy of distribution shift patterns specific to clinical data.
futureDirection: Developing practical frameworks for uncertainty communication in clinical decision support — specifically, how to surface model confidence in a form that is actionable for practitioners rather than technically accurate but clinically opaque.
